RKNN: a caller may receive another thread's result

### I have searched the existing issues, both open and closed, to make sure this is not a duplicate report.

### The bug

Description:
Summary
- The current RKNN pool implementation in machine-learning/immich_ml/sessions/rknn/rknnpool.py uses a shared queue and separate put() and get() methods. When multiple threads call RknnSession.run concurrently, put()/get() pairs can interleave and a caller may receive another thread's result. ### Feature Description

OpenRouter returns the serving backend as a top-level `provider` field on chat
completions. `ChatOpenRouter` drops it, so there is no way to tell which backend
served a request.

The same prompt sent twice with default routing — once against the HTTP API to
show what the wire returns, once through the integration:

```python
import json
import os

import httpx
from langchain_openrouter import ChatOpenRouter

KEY = os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]
MODEL = "meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b-instruct"
MSG = [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 2+2?"}]

d = httpx.post(
    "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}"},
    json={"model": MODEL, "messages": MSG},
    timeout=60,
).json()
print("--- raw HTTP response (choices omitted) ---")
print(json.dumps({k: v for k, v in d.items() if k != "choices"}, indent=2))

resp = ChatOpenRouter(model=MODEL, openrouter_api_key=KEY).invoke(MSG)
print("--- ChatOpenRouter response_metadata ---")
print(json.dumps(resp.response_metadata, indent=2, default=str))
```

```
--- raw HTTP response (choices omitted) ---
{
  "id": "gen-1786003718-HRoJ0jUzGm8nyrROAuro",
  "object": "chat.completion",
  "created": 1786003718,
  "model": "meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b-instruct",
  "provider": "Novita",
  "system_fingerprint": null,
  "service_tier": null,
  "usage": {
    "prompt_tokens": 18,
    "completion_tokens": 8,
    "total_tokens": 26,
    "cost": 7.6e-07,
    "is_byok": false,
    "prompt_tokens_details": {
      "cached_tokens": 0,
      "cache_write_tokens": 0,
      "audio_tokens": 0,
      "video_tokens": 0
    },
    "cost_details": {
      "upstream_inference_cost": 7.6e-07,
      "upstream_inference_prompt_cost": 3.6e-07,
      "upstream_inference_completions_cost": 4e-07
    },
    "completion_tokens_details": {
      "reasoning_tokens": 0,
      "image_tokens": 0,
      "audio_tokens": 0
    }
  }
}
--- ChatOpenRouter response_metadata ---
{
  "model_name": "meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b-instruct",
  "id": "gen-1786003719-TXndPAGhhttfoE1qWcr3",
  "created": 1786003719,
  "object": "chat.completion",
  "finish_reason": "stop",
  "logprobs": null,
  "model_provider": "openrouter",
  "cost": 6.6e-07,
  "cost_details": {
    "upstream_inference_completions_cost": 3.2e-07,
    "upstream_inference_prompt_cost": 3.4e-07,
    "upstream_inference_cost": 6.6e-07
  }
}
```

Every other top-level field is carried across — `id`, `object`, `created`,
`model`, plus `cost` / `cost_details` lifted out of the nested `usage` object.
Only `provider` is dropped. `model_provider` is the constant `"openrouter"`,
which is correct as integration identity but doesn't say which backend ran.

The two calls above also landed on different backends. Same model, same prompt,
a second apart — `GET /api/v1/generation` reports `Novita` for the raw one and
`DeepInfra` for the LangChain one, which is why the costs differ (`7.6e-07` vs
`6.6e-07`). That is `allow_fallbacks` working as designed. The point is that
nothing in `response_metadata` distinguishes the two.

Pinning confirms the field reports the real backend rather than echoing the
request: with `openrouter_provider={"only": ["DeepInfra"]}` the raw response says
`"provider": "DeepInfra"` where the default-routed one said `"Novita"`, and
`response_metadata` has the same shape as above — still no `provider` key.

`_create_chat_result` reads `model` and `system_fingerprint` off the top level
(`chat_models.py:836-838`) but never `provider`. The streaming paths hardcode
`generation_info["model_provider"] = "openrouter"` (`:651`, `:736`) and don't
read it either. The value is discarded while the `AIMessage` is built, so
callbacks, logs and LangSmith never get the chance — they faithfully record
metadata the field has already been stripped from.

Worth flagging: `provider` isn't in OpenRouter's documented response schema,
though it's present on every live response I've made and is the same value
`GET /api/v1/generation` returns. A truthy guard makes an absent field a no-op,
as `system_fingerprint` already is.

### Use Case

I run claim-verification workloads through OpenRouter with `allow_fallbacks` on,
so any call can land on one of several backends that don't always share the same
quantization. When output quality shifts, the first question is which backend
served the affected runs — and that's unanswerable today.

The gap isn't limited to output quality. Latency and cost vary by backend the
same way, and we're exploring blind on all of it — even with LangSmith in place.
It faithfully records the cost and latency of every run; what it can't record is
the one variable that would explain why they differ. Two runs of the same model
with different numbers look identical in the trace.

What does get recorded is the request side — `openrouter_provider` shows up in
trace metadata — which is what you asked for, never what served you. With
fallbacks on those two diverge exactly when it matters, as they did by accident
in the snippet above.

### Proposed Solution

Read `provider` where the other top-level response fields are already read, and
apply it beside `system_fingerprint`:

```python
response_model = response.get("model")
system_fingerprint = response.get("system_fingerprint")
serving_provider = response.get("provider")  # new

...

if isinstance(message, AIMessage):
    if system_fingerprint:
        message.response_metadata["system_fingerprint"] = system_fingerprint
    if serving_provider:                                   # new
        message.response_metadata["provider"] = serving_provider
```

Plus the equivalent in the two streaming paths. Unit-testable without network by
passing a response dict to `_create_chat_result`.

Open question on the key name: `provider` matches the wire format but sits next
to `model_provider: "openrouter"` and could read as contradictory.
`upstream_provider` or `serving_provider` disambiguate. Happy either way.

### Alternatives Considered

- **`ChatOpenAI` with OpenRouter's `base_url`** (our current setup) — drops
  `provider` too, and misreports `ls_provider` as `"openai"`. #34962 covered this.
- **Pin one provider and disable fallbacks** — then you know, but you give up the
  routing availability that's the reason to use OpenRouter.
- **A follow-up `GET /api/v1/generation?id=<id>` per call** — this is how I
  identified the two backends above, so it works, but it's an extra round trip
  and arrives too late to attach to the run.
- **A local subclass overriding `_create_chat_result`** — what we'll do meanwhile.
  Three lines against a private method that every user needing provenance has to
  write themselves.

### Additional Context

The RFC that led to this package, #34962, named this as a motivation:

> - Loses OpenRouter-specific metadata (which provider served the request)
> - Breaks LangSmith traces with incorrect provider attribution

The package landed shortly after in #35211, but the field itself wasn't carried
through. #37137 (`session_id` / `trace`) is the closest precedent for surfacing
OpenRouter-specific metadata. Verified against `langchain-openrouter==0.2.7`.

Happy to open the PR — just let me know on the key name and assign me.

[Bug]: Reachable remote server is shown as Ready without a workspace window

### Operating system

macOS

### Orca version

Observed with a 1.4.167 client connected to a 1.4.150 host. The runtime protocol versions were compatible.

### Details

**Short summary**

A paired Remote Orca Server can remain reachable after its workspace window/renderer graph becomes unavailable. In that state, project Settings still labels the host setup **Ready**, and the status bar still presents the server as ordinarily connected, even though interactive workspace actions cannot use the missing renderer graph.

**What happened?**

The host runtime remained reachable and returned status successfully, but reported:

- `graphStatus: unavailable`
- `desktopWindowStatus: openable`

Settings > Project > Available Hosts nevertheless showed the remote setup as **Ready**. Attempting graph-dependent terminal actions then failed instead of explaining that Orca needed to be opened on the host. Opening Orca on the host restored the graph immediately.

**How can we reproduce it?**

1. Pair a desktop Orca client with a headed Remote Orca Server.
2. Close the server's workspace window while leaving its main process/runtime reachable.
3. Confirm the server reports an unavailable graph and an openable desktop window.
4. Open the project's **Available Hosts** settings or the status-bar remote-host menu.
5. Observe that the setup is still shown as **Ready/Connected** rather than identifying the unavailable workspace window.

**Expected behavior**

A reachable server without a usable workspace renderer should have a distinct, actionable state—for example, **Open Orca** / **Workspace window closed**—without being mislabeled as network-disconnected.

**Roadmap context**

This report is intentionally narrower than the ongoing work to remove the renderer dependency:

- #8300 keeps serving remote clients by optionally hiding rather than destroying the headed renderer.
- #6844 introduces an Electron-free headless server.

Those changes can prevent this state in more configurations. This issue only tracks truthful status for current, legacy, and degraded headed servers while the runtime explicitly reports that its desktop window is openable but its graph is unavailable.

The separate terminal-surface race present on the older host build was resolved by updating the host and is not the scope of this report.

[Bug]: Architecture component-level failures report empty subject/evidence/supportedFixes while their messages carry the repair

## Problem

`architecture` renderer diagnostics for component-level failures arrive with every structured field empty, even though each message already carries the measured repair. With `validate --json`:

- `subject` is only `{"diagramType":"architecture"}` — it does not name the affected component (or pair),
- `evidence` is `{}` — none of the numbers the message itself already computed,
- `supportedFixes` is `[]` — although the message ends in a concrete repair, e.g. `Suggested fix: move "right" pos to [248, 40] (right of "left") or [244, 128] (below)`.

`references/authoring-contract.md` tells agents to "Consume `diagnostics[]` by stable `code`, exact `subject`, measured `evidence`, and `supportedFixes`". For these four failure kinds the documented repair loop has nothing to act on and the free-text message is the only signal, while the sibling families already carry the fields — `layout/boundary-out-of-bounds`, `layout/route-out-of-bounds`, `composition/label-gap` in the same renderer, and `sequence/participant-label-overflow` in the sequence renderer.

Affected kinds (all fall back to the untyped `layout/constraint` default):

1. Component falls outside the viewBox.
2. Two components closer than 8px (the message already includes a two-coordinate suggestion).
3. Label wider than its component.
4. Sublabel/tag unreadable at the legible minimum.

## Reproduction

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "diagram_type": "architecture",
  "meta": { "title": "Component diagnostics probe", "output": "probe.html", "quality_profile": "standard", "viewBox": [640, 360] },
  "components": [
    { "id": "left",    "type": "backend",  "label": "Left", "pos": [40, 40],   "size": [200, 80] },
    { "id": "right",   "type": "backend",  "label": "Right", "pos": [244, 40],  "size": [200, 80] },
    { "id": "outside", "type": "database", "label": "Outside", "pos": [520, 300], "size": [200, 80] },
    { "id": "narrow",  "type": "backend",  "label": "A Deliberately Long Label", "pos": [40, 180], "size": [56, 80], "sublabel": "A very long sublabel that cannot possibly fit" }
  ],
  "connections": []
}
```

`node archify/bin/archify.mjs validate architecture <file> --json` → 4 diagnostics, each
`code: "layout/constraint"`, `subject: {"diagramType":"architecture"}`, `evidence: {}`, `supportedFixes: []`.

## Actual (verbatim messages; the fields shown above are empty on all four)

1. `Component "outside" falls outside the viewBox 640x360 — adjust pos/size or set a larger meta.viewBox.`
2. `Label "A Deliberately Long Label" (~165px) is wider than component "narrow" (56px) — shorten the label or widen size.`
3. `Sublabel "A very long sublabel that cannot possibly fit" needs ~162px at the 6px legible minimum, but component "narrow" provides 48px — shorten the sublabel or widen size.`
4. Multi-line: `Components "left" and "right" are less than 8px apart — move one or shrink its size.` plus the two-line bounds/suggestion hint.

The same empty fields appear in `render`/`deliver` failure receipts, under `layout.mode: "grid"`, and under `quality_profile: "showcase"`.

## Expected

The four kinds carry the affected component (or pair) in `subject`, the numbers the message already computes in `evidence`, and the concrete repair(s) in `supportedFixes`, following the same contract as the sibling diagnostics listed above.

[Bug]: Standalone SVG retains Viewer width rules when opened directly

## Problem

Opening a Viewer-exported SVG directly in Chromium lets the embedded Viewer CSS override its intrinsic width without adjusting its height. The outer SVG viewport therefore changes aspect ratio with the browser window.

This came up in [the review of #272](https://github.com/tt-a1i/archify/pull/272#discussion_r4030640337), but reproduces on untouched `dev` at `53bc4e19b0d82993609110b865d47178fccd5004`. The Viewer and CLI outputs from `3abe10bb203cd82950219d9c8da0842062d170c5` behave identically. Tracking it separately avoids changing existing Viewer export behaviour as part of CLI parity work.

## Reproduction

From a source checkout at the `dev` commit above:

```sh
out=$(mktemp -d)
node archify/bin/archify.mjs deliver architecture \
  archify/examples/web-app.architecture.json "$out/viewer.html" --json
```

Use the checked-in `web-app.architecture.json` unchanged. Open the HTML, export SVG from the Viewer, then open the downloaded SVG directly. In browser DevTools, set the viewport to 640×900 and 1440×900 and run:

```js
const svg = document.documentElement;
const bounds = svg.getBoundingClientRect();
({
  viewBox: svg.getAttribute('viewBox'),
  width: svg.getAttribute('width'),
  height: svg.getAttribute('height'),
  rendered: [bounds.width, bounds.height],
  minWidth: getComputedStyle(svg).minWidth
});
```

## Observed result

The root declares `viewBox="0 0 1080 588"`, `width="1080"` and `height="588"`. Its measured size is **640×588** in the first viewport and **1440×588** in the second, on both revisions. Delivery and deterministic checks pass.

The exported stylesheet includes:

```css
svg {
  width: 100%;
  min-width: min(900px, 100%);
}
```

This concerns the outer viewport, not a claim that shapes are stretched: the default SVG aspect-ratio behaviour still applies to the diagram content. Image/canvas parity at explicit intrinsic dimensions does not exercise this top-level-document case.

## Expected behaviour / scope

Standalone exports should have a deliberate sizing policy: either honour the intrinsic dimensions or scale responsively while preserving the viewport ratio. Please confirm the preferred behaviour before changing the shared export path. Keep the interactive Viewer's layout unchanged, and cover direct SVG navigation as well as raster export when fixing it.

Environment: Linux, Node 22.23.2, Chromium 153.0.8010.36; source checkout. No other browser engines tested. Codex assisted with the reproduction and report.

eth_newFilter rejects earliest-to-earliest ranges while eth_getLogs accepts them

#### System information

Geth version: `Geth/v1.17.8-stable-a5790770/darwin-arm64/go1.25.1`  
CL client & version: None; isolated reproduction at genesis without syncing or mining.  
OS & Version: macOS 26.5.1, ARM64  
Commit hash: `a579077007b98217c3e253a66e4b452ca0c32b96` (v1.17.8)

Both clients were tested using fresh data directories with Ethereum mainnet genesis, chain ID 1, no peers, and block height 0.

Comparison client: Reth v2.7.0, commit `3d592ece6de8c4559987416a544fc215fd6d6921`.

#### Expected behaviour

In this fresh, unpruned environment, creating a filter with `fromBlock: "earliest"` and `toBlock: "earliest"` should succeed, consistently with the equivalent `"0x0"` range and with `eth_getLogs` using the same tags.

Querying the resulting filter with `eth_getFilterLogs` should return `[]`, since the genesis block contains no logs.

If rejecting this range is intentional, could you clarify why `eth_newFilter` handles it differently from `eth_getLogs`?

#### Actual behaviour

Geth rejects the filter during `eth_newFilter`:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"error":{"code":-32602,"message":"invalid block range params"}}
```

No filter ID is returned, so there is no subsequent valid `eth_getFilterLogs` call for this case.

The following results were consistent across three repetitions:

| Request | Geth v1.17.8 | Reth v2.7.0 |
|---|---|---|
| `eth_newFilter`, `earliest` → `earliest` | `-32602: invalid block range params` | Returns a filter ID |
| `eth_getFilterLogs` for that filter | Not applicable; creation failed | `[]` |
| `eth_getLogs`, `earliest` → `earliest` | `[]` | `[]` |
| `eth_newFilter`, `0x0` → `0x0` | Returns a filter ID | Returns a filter ID |
| `eth_newFilter`, `latest` → `latest` | Returns a filter ID | Returns a filter ID |

**Possible cause**

In Geth, [`EarliestBlockNumber` is represented internally as `-5`](https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/blob/a579077007b98217c3e253a66e4b452ca0c32b96/rpc/types.go#L66-L72).

In [`SubscribeLogs`](https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/blob/a579077007b98217c3e253a66e4b452ca0c32b96/eth/filters/filter_system.go#L328-L348), `from == rpc.EarliestBlockNumber` is converted to `HistoryPruningCutoff()`, but the corresponding conversion is not applied to `to`.

In this environment, the resulting range is therefore `from = 0`, `to = -5`, which fails the subsequent range checks. This appears to be an asymmetric tag normalization issue.

For comparison, Reth [installs the filter at creation](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/blob/3d592ece6de8c4559987416a544fc215fd6d6921/crates/rpc/rpc/src/eth/filter.rs#L358-L364), then [applies `convert_block_number` to both bounds when querying logs](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/blob/3d592ece6de8c4559987416a544fc215fd6d6921/crates/rpc/rpc/src/eth/filter.rs#L594-L605). report:
[bug] Combined unlisten from onDragDropEvent / onFocusChanged discards inner promises, causing unhandled rejections

### Describe the bug

Several `@tauri-apps/api` helpers register multiple event listeners and return one combined cleanup (`UnlistenFn`) function. That combined cleanup calls each inner unlisten function but discards the promises they return:

```ts
// packages/api/src/webview.ts — Webview.onDragDropEvent
return () => {
  unlistenDragEnter()
  unlistenDragDrop()
  unlistenDragOver()
  unlistenDragLeave()
}
```

Each inner unlisten comes from `listen()` and is `async () => _unlisten(event, eventId)`. It can reject, for example when the listener was already removed, or when the `plugin:event|unlisten` invoke fails.

Because the combined cleanup returns `undefined`, callers have nothing to `await` or `.catch()`, so a rejection surfaces as an **unhandled promise rejection**. This commonly happens on React unmount, when cleanup races listener registration or teardown. A production app saw thousands of these.

Affected APIs (verified still present on `dev` and in `@tauri-apps/api` 2.12.0):

- `Webview.onDragDropEvent` — `packages/api/src/webview.ts` (4 listeners)
- `Window.onDragDropEvent` — `packages/api/src/window.ts` (4 listeners: drag, drop, dragOver, cancel)
- `Window.onFocusChanged` — `packages/api/src/window.ts` (2 listeners: focus, blur)

A grep of `packages/api/src` for `return () => { unlistenX(); ... }` finds no other combined cleanups besides these three.

Note: this is distinct from #15799, which was about a single `unlisten` throwing internally. Even a correctly-rejecting single unlisten is unobservable here because the combined wrapper drops its promise.

### Reproduction

```ts
import { getCurrentWebview } from '@tauri-apps/api/webview'

// 1. Register a combined listener
const unlisten = await getCurrentWebview().onDragDropEvent(() => {})

// 2. Call the combined cleanup when one of the underlying listeners is
//    already gone — e.g. after the webview listener was torn down,
//    or call cleanup twice — so an inner _unlisten rejects:
//      TypeError: undefined is not an object
//        (evaluating 'listeners[eventId].handlerId')
//    or the `plugin:event|unlisten` invoke fails.
unlisten()

// 3. Observe: there is no promise to await/catch on the returned cleanup,
//    so the inner rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection.
```

The same pattern reproduces with `getCurrentWindow().onDragDropEvent(...)` and `getCurrentWindow().onFocusChanged(...)`, and in practice via a React effect cleanup on unmount racing teardown.

### Expected behavior

The combined cleanup should return one promise that settles once every inner unlisten has run, e.g.:

```ts
return async () => {
  await Promise.all([
    unlistenDragEnter(),
    unlistenDragDrop(),
    unlistenDragOver(),
    unlistenDragLeave()
  ])
}
```

`UnlistenFn` is typed `() => void`, so an async function stays assignable and the public type does not change. Callers that ignore the result behave as before; callers that `await` or `.catch()` it can now handle failures. All inner unlistens still start synchronously, same as today.

### Full `tauri info` output

Not from a full app reproduction — the bug is visible directly in the `@tauri-apps/api` sources:

```
@tauri-apps/api 2.12.0 (also present on dev at time of filing)
packages/api/src/webview.ts: Webview.onDragDropEvent
packages/api/src/window.ts: Window.onDragDropEvent, Window.onFocusChanged
```

### Stack trace

```text
TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'listeners[eventId].handlerId')
  — raised inside an inner async unlisten, surfaced as an unhandled promise rejection
    because the combined cleanup returned undefined
```

### Additional context

- `Promise.allSettled` plus rethrowing the first error is an alternative if maintainers prefer that every failure be observed.
- Separately, a rejected intermediate `await this.listen(...)` inside these helpers leaks the listeners registered before it. That is a possible follow-up and is not part of this report's proposed fix.

## Area

Setup, packaging, or upgrade; generated artifacts and validation.

A successful cached build restored a package whose generated TypeScript catalog was current but whose compiled generated catalog contained older input/output definitions. Direct conversion of all 139 canonical contracts matched the generated source. The compiled artifact differed at 78 leaf locations across seven tools: `observe_native_calls`, `trace_dylib_resolution`, `analyze_javascript_application`, `trace_javascript_semantics`, `observe_web_execution`, `inspect_web_event_listeners`, and `binary_session`.

A real stdio `tools/list` call against the same baseline advertised all 139 tools and matched the freshly generated source for every input/output schema, while differing from the stale compiled artifact for exactly those seven tools. The initial report incorrectly described the generated file as the server's source. No stale-schema client failure is established; the report now concerns generated-artifact consistency and unnecessary package contents.

## Reproduction

1. Build a checkout, then change a canonical schema or update to a revision with schema changes while retaining previously generated catalog source.
2. Run `npm run build:cached` once.
3. Compare `dist/generatedMcpToolCatalog.js` with the current generated source and canonical post-SDK contracts.
4. Also connect to the built production MCP server and compare the actual `tools/list` result, rather than assuming it consumes the compiled generated module.

Observed at `cc0ee2edc60dda42d7b7cfb2c08e39b0b736b5e9`:

```json
  "live_matches_fresh_generated_source": true,
  "compiled_generated_matches_fresh_source": false,
  "live_vs_stale_compiled_difference_tools": 7
}
```

## Expected behavior

Generated artifacts included in a package should match the current build. If an artifact exists only for source-level schema/conformance tests, consider excluding its compiled form from the shipping package instead of adding unnecessary runtime generation or compilation. Preserve the useful generated source tests.

## Impact and scope

The package contains a stale, unused generated module, and the current source generator check does not validate its compiled form. Source-level tests can pass while this unused compiled output drifts. The observed module was about 6.7 MB on disk; compressed archive impact has not yet been measured independently.

Actual live discovery/validation continues to use the registered canonical contracts. Existing production MCP behavior, target Evidence, graph identity and full real Notion/Obsidian analyses remain unaffected by this compiled-file discrepancy.

## REA version

Source revision `cc0ee2edc60dda42d7b7cfb2c08e39b0b736b5e9`; package version 6.0.0. This is a concrete build observation, not a claim about every published package.

## Runtime and platform

Linux x64, Node.js 24.18.0; package-file inspection also performed on native Windows x64, Node.js 22.19.0. This generation boundary is not Windows-specific.

## Target and artifact context

Generated MCP catalog source and compiled package output. Discovered during actual complete Notion/Obsidian verification for #1065/#1112. Target code is unnecessary for a reduced regression.

## Interface

Build/package and generated-schema validation.

## Earliest failure stage

Compiled generated artifact consistency. Actual production `tools/list` was verified current.

## Relevant output or evidence

The stale artifact contained 2,030,334 serialized characters versus 2,035,845 for the freshly generated source. Structural comparison, not byte count, established the mismatch. A separate real stdio consumer check verified all 139 current advertised input/output schemas.

One build should produce internally consistent necessary artifacts. Do not add runtime errors or user configuration to address an unused build artifact.

## Analysis or suspected cause

`build:unlocked` compiles TypeScript before `generate-mcp-tool-catalog.mjs` writes its updated TypeScript source. An older existing source can therefore be compiled before regeneration, and this compiled output can be cached. The generated catalog is used by source-level tests; current production registration uses named contracts and `toolRegistrationOptions` directly. Exact cache population history was not reconstructed.

- Related roadmap: #1065 T3; package storage and generated conformance boundaries.
- #1076 moved derived outputs out of Git; preserve that design.
- #1001 concerns missing generated shard inputs and is distinct.
- #919 requires checking the representation actually consumed by clients; that check corrected this report's original impact assumption.

Acceptance: seed older generated source and run one build/cache restoration; verify the necessary generated test source remains current, compiled/package outputs contain only appropriate current artifacts, actual packaged `tools/list` matches post-SDK contracts, and inventory/identity/packaged skill metadata agree. Keep the build/resource budget small.

Seven hook-rewritten commands skip the hook integrity check (aws, psql, wc, mypy, gradlew, mvn, mvnd)

Seven commands the hook rewrites into skip the hook integrity check: `aws`, `psql`, `wc`, `mypy`, `gradlew`, `mvn` and `mvnd`. They are missing from `is_operational_command` in `src/main.rs`, which is an explicit whitelist ("a forgotten command fails open").

With a legacy `~/.claude/hooks/rtk-rewrite.sh` whose content no longer matches `.rtk-hook.sha256`, `rtk git status` and `rtk vitest` stop with `rtk: hook integrity check FAILED` and exit 1, while these seven go on to run the tool (`rtk wc -l` prints its count; the others reach their tool lookup). Each one is a command `rtk rewrite` produces:

```
aws s3 ls         -> rtk aws s3 ls
psql -c 'select 1' -> rtk psql -c 'select 1'
wc -l src/main.rs -> rtk wc -l src/main.rs
mypy src          -> rtk mypy src
./gradlew build   -> rtk gradlew build
mvn test          -> rtk mvn test
mvnd test         -> rtk mvnd test
```

`jest` had the same gap; #2418 adds it.

The list drifts because it is opt-in: a new command is unchecked until someone remembers it. An exhaustive `match` over `Commands` (meta commands listed as `false` by name, no `_` arm) makes the compiler ask for a decision on every new variant, and a test can assert that every command `rtk rewrite` emits is operational.

### Related Issues / PRs

Same broader defect class raised in #40001 ("AIMessage.content_blocks mutates message.content in the Anthropic, Bedrock and Google translators"), which explicitly identified this exact Anthropic-translator case. #40001 was closed as completed after #40022 (bedrock_converse fix) and #40023 (google-genai fix) merged, but neither of those touches anthropic.py -- this specific half was never fixed. bedrock.py's _convert_to_v1_from_bedrock() imports and calls _convert_to_v1_from_anthropic() directly, so model_provider="bedrock" (for Claude-backed models) inherits the same bug.

### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python)

```python
from copy import deepcopy

from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage

message = AIMessage(
    content=[{"type": "custom", "payload": "value", "index": 3}],
    response_metadata={"model_provider": "anthropic"},
)
original = deepcopy(message.content)

first = message.content_blocks  # first read

print("before:", original)
print("after: ", message.content)
assert message.content == original  # fails: `index` is gone
```

### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable)

```shell
N/A -- not an exception, silent data corruption.

AssertionError: assert [{'type': 'custom', 'payload': 'value'}] == [{'type': 'custom', 'payload': 'value', 'index': 3}]
```

### Description

`_convert_to_v1_from_anthropic` in `libs/core/langchain_core/messages/block_translators/anthropic.py` builds most content blocks as fresh dicts, but the fallback `else` branch for an unrecognized block type wraps the original block by reference and then pops a key off it: it builds `new_block["value"] = block` (the same dict, not a copy) and then does `new_block["value"].pop("index")`. Since `new_block["value"]` is `block`, the original dict living inside `message.content`, that pop deletes `index` from the message's own stored content as a side effect of reading the read-only-looking `.content_blocks` property.

Impact. A message that carries a non-standard content block with an `index` key silently loses that key the first time `.content_blocks` is read, e.g. from logging, middleware, or a second unrelated call site. Anything that persists or re-serializes `message.content` afterward (checkpointers, conversation stores, `dumps()`) captures the corrupted version. `bedrock.py`'s `_convert_to_v1_from_bedrock` imports and calls this same function directly, so `model_provider="bedrock"` for Claude-backed models inherits the identical bug (confirmed locally).

Proposed fix: copy the block before popping `index` off it, exactly the pattern already accepted for the analogous Bedrock Converse fix (#40022, in `bedrock_converse.py`) -- `value = block.copy()`, pop `index` from `value`, and build the `non_standard` wrapper (with the lifted `index`) from that copy instead of from `block` directly. I already have this implemented with regression tests for both the `anthropic` and `bedrock` providers (message content provably unchanged after one or more `.content_blocks` reads) and verified locally: full `langchain-core` unit suite passing (2256 passed), `ruff check`/`ruff format --diff`/`mypy` clean, import-linter clean. ## Root cause
The four sandbox shell tools (`shell_run`, `shell_wait`, `shell_input`, `shell_interrupt`) in `dify-agent/src/dify_agent/layers/shell/layer.py` (~L251) are registered without docstrings, so no description is derived. The adapter in `dify-agent/src/dify_agent/adapters/llm/model.py` (L554) then sends `description=""`. The Bedrock Converse API enforces `minLength: 1` on `toolSpec.description` and rejects the whole request. The `system[2].text` error is an analogous empty system/instruction block.

This makes Agent (Beta) unusable with any Bedrock model whenever the shell layer is active, independent of user-configured tools.

## Suggested fix
Add descriptions to the shell layer tools and/or use a non-empty fallback in `_map_tool_definitions_to_prompt_tools`; filter empty system text blocks before sending.

## Description

Update (2026-08-11): I also tested the `8e74d7d715c88f1bd0a681cb275a8f7811522c97` implementation on a self-hosted Linux Dify deployment using the exact deployed Agent backend and Go/Rust sandbox images. The production-host, full Agent v2 shadow A/B below complements (and does not replace) the matched-container microbenchmarks above.

Update (2026-08-08): I rebased the experiment on current Dify `main` at `60d6be5b137bc021364f4b4a9bce268a58e9b439`, ported the protocol-compatible Rust runtime to that tree, fixed the benchmark methodology, optimized the Rust implementation, and reran correctness and performance tests. This update supersedes all numbers previously shown in this issue.

Related work:

- [#38671 — Go prototype with lower idle memory and faster startup](https://github.com/langgenius/dify/issues/38671)
- [#38841 — migrate the Python shell runtime to Go](https://github.com/langgenius/dify/pull/38841)

This is not a proposal to rewrite Dify in Rust. It asks whether a narrowly scoped, protocol-compatible Rust implementation of `dify-agent-runtime` is worth pursuing, given the maintenance cost of another toolchain.

The prototype implements the current shell runtime HTTP contract and the four runtime helpers (`shellctl`, PTY sanitizer, runner, and runner-exit). The production image uses the same Python 3.12 slim base and the same Node, pnpm, uv, tmux, and CLI tooling as the Go image. The implementation also preserves tmux job supervision, SQLite state, interactive input, output offsets, termination/deletion, and Linux Landlock behavior.

### Correction to the previous memory claim

The earlier revision compared historical Python, Go, and Rust server-process RSS values from unlike process boundaries. In particular, tmux and container memory were not accounted for consistently, and the earlier Rust prototype did not yet keep the current persistent tmux server behavior. Therefore the previous “8.81x lower than Python” and related idle-memory ratios should be treated as invalid for a whole-runtime comparison.

The corrected matched-container result is substantially smaller: final Rust uses **48.4% less long-lived-process RSS than Go (1.94x)** in the Linux container test. Depending on the container memory definition, the measured reduction is **56.8% for cgroup `memory.current`** or **68.6% for Docker's displayed working set**. These definitions are reported separately and should not be mixed.

## Motivation

### Reproducible benchmark design

- Host: Apple Silicon, Docker Desktop 29.2.1; benchmark containers are Linux/arm64.
- Runtime images: Go and Rust use identical production tooling and are limited to 2 CPUs and 1 GiB RAM.
- Seven independent paired rounds; execution order alternates `go,rust` and `rust,go`.
- Each round includes one cold job, five untimed warmups, 50 sequential jobs, 12 jobs returning at least 32 KiB, and 25 jobs through 8 workers.
- Every timed job must return `done=true`, `status=exited`, `exit_code=0`, and the expected output; failures abort the comparison.
- Values below are medians of the seven round-level medians. Reduction confidence intervals use a deterministic 10,000-resample paired bootstrap.
- Memory is sampled separately as cgroup `memory.current`, Docker working set, and RSS of long-lived processes (`tini` + runtime server + tmux). The short-lived `ps` sampler is explicitly excluded.
- Reports record raw samples, image IDs, source SHA-256 digests, repository SHA/status, runtime order, and tool versions.

Lower is better for every metric below.

| Linux container metric | Go median | Final Rust median | Go/Rust | Rust reduction (95% CI) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Cold first real job | 126.735 ms | **26.766 ms** | 4.60x | **78.3%** [73.8%, 81.4%] |
| 50 sequential real jobs | 125.779 ms | **21.549 ms** | 5.78x | **82.7%** [82.3%, 83.2%] |
| 32 KiB output job | 175.354 ms | **30.549 ms** | 5.82x | **82.8%** [82.1%, 82.9%] |
| 8-worker concurrent jobs | 119.057 ms | **20.025 ms** | 5.90x | **83.1%** [82.2%, 83.5%] |
| Startup to healthy | 164.324 ms | 160.725 ms | 1.01x | 1.0% [-7.8%, 6.5%] |
| Idle long-lived-process RSS | 17.008 MiB | **8.770 MiB** | 1.94x | **48.4%** [48.4%, 48.5%] |
| Idle cgroup `memory.current` | 7.830 MiB | **3.309 MiB** | 2.31x | **56.8%** [56.2%, 58.1%] |
| Idle Docker working set | 6.723 MiB | **2.105 MiB** | 3.19x | **68.6%** [67.8%, 68.8%] |
| Post-workload cgroup memory | 19.943 MiB | **11.088 MiB** | 1.79x | **44.3%** [43.6%, 45.5%] |

There is no statistically supported startup improvement: its confidence interval crosses zero.

### Rust optimization A/B on the same Dify revision

I preserved the pre-optimization Rust image and reran both images with the corrected harness. Each side has seven independent paired Go/Rust rounds. To control for host drift, the A/B result first computes Rust/Go within every round and then compares those ratios across the pre/final runs.

| Metric | Pre-optimization Rust | Final Rust | Direct Rust speedup | Go-normalized speedup (95% CI) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sequential real job | 69.969 ms | **21.549 ms** | 3.25x | **3.29x** [3.19x, 3.48x] |
| 32 KiB output job | 68.900 ms | **30.549 ms** | 2.26x | **2.31x** [2.19x, 2.37x] |
| 8-worker concurrent jobs | 67.343 ms | **20.025 ms** | 3.36x | **3.35x** [3.08x, 3.48x] |
| Cold first job | 73.987 ms | **26.766 ms** | 2.76x | **2.68x** [1.58x, 3.18x] |
| Idle long-lived-process RSS | 9.023 MiB | **8.770 MiB** | 1.03x | **1.03x** [1.02x, 1.17x] |
| Startup to healthy | 153.561 ms | 160.725 ms | 0.96x | 0.98x [0.86x, 1.05x] |

The main latency changes were:

1. poll cheap atomic completion artifacts every 5 ms while retaining the expensive tmux liveness fallback at 50 ms;
2. avoid two unconditional tmux liveness probes at the beginning of every wait;
3. combine `new-session` and `pipe-pane` into one tmux client invocation;
4. reuse the sanitizer output buffer and avoid flushing every 8 KiB chunk;
5. use a current-thread Tokio runtime for the lightweight HTTP server; and
6. enable thin LTO, one codegen unit, and symbol stripping for release builds.

The result is primarily a short-job/process-management improvement, not an LLM, database, vector-search, or provider-latency benchmark. Long-running wait CPU overhead and production-scale mixed workloads still need dedicated profiling before any adoption decision.

### Self-hosted Linux full Agent v2 shadow A/B (2026-08-11)

To check whether the runtime microbenchmark gains survive the real Agent v2 orchestration path, I ran an isolated A/B on a self-hosted Linux Dify host.

Method:

- Dify source revision: `8e74d7d715c88f1bd0a681cb275a8f7811522c97`.
- Exact deployed images: Agent backend `local/dify-agent-backend:8e74d7d-rust-canary-v3`, Go sandbox `langgenius/dify-agent-local-sandbox:1.16.1`, and Rust sandbox `local/dify-agent-local-sandbox-rust:8e74d7d-canary-v1`.
- Temporary, unexposed shadow containers ran on the production host's internal Docker network. They had no host ports and received no production traffic; the production containers were not restarted.
- The benchmark exercised the full `/execution-bindings` → `/runs` → events/status → `/workspace/files/read` → binding-destroy path.
- A deterministic in-process model removed provider latency while retaining the Agent v2 tool loop.
- Two warm-up pairs were followed by 20 measured paired samples with alternating Go-first/Rust-first order and a fresh binding/workspace for every sample.
- Every run executed five sequential shell actions: marker creation, 32 KiB file creation, SHA-256, 32 KiB stdout, and final file verification.
- The model validated every tool result, including completion state, exit code, and content, and called `shell_wait` whenever `done=false`.
- Confidence intervals use a deterministic paired bootstrap with 10,000 resamples.

| Full Agent v2 metric | Go median | Rust median | Go/Rust | Rust reduction (95% CI) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Binding create | 187.236 ms | **41.883 ms** | 4.470x | **77.6%** [70.0%, 79.0%] |
| Agent run | 882.419 ms | **290.734 ms** | 3.035x | **67.1%** [66.8%, 68.5%] |
| 32 KiB file read | 424.267 ms | **150.012 ms** | 2.828x | **64.6%** [63.4%, 65.4%] |
| Binding destroy | 134.766 ms | **36.042 ms** | 3.739x | **73.3%** [72.6%, 73.6%] |
| Full session | 1,999.212 ms | **670.795 ms** | 2.980x | **66.4%** [65.8%, 67.4%] |

Rust was faster in all 20 paired full-session samples (two-sided sign test, `p ≈ 1.91e-6`). Full-session p95 was 2,126.475 ms for Go and 691.185 ms for Rust.

Runtime observations:

- Go required 13 `shell_wait` calls over 20 sessions (median 1 per session); Rust required 1 total (median 0).
- Go produced one `done=true`, `exit_code=0`, `status=lost` terminal anomaly; Rust produced none. The output still passed strict content validation, and the anomaly was counted separately.
- Immediately before the temporary sandboxes were removed, the Go container used 26.39 MiB with 802 PIDs and 783 zombie `sh`/`tmux` processes; Rust used 4.766 MiB with 4 PIDs and no zombies. This is a post-workload diagnostic snapshot, **not** a controlled idle-memory benchmark, so it should not replace the matched idle-memory results above.

Safety/cleanup checks:

- The production Agent backend, Go sandbox, and Rust sandbox retained their original container IDs, start times, and restart count of zero.
- Dify still returned HTTP 200 and both production sandbox `/healthz` endpoints passed after the benchmark.
- All temporary containers, workspaces, homes, and shellctl job records were absent after cleanup.

This measures the runtime-dependent Agent v2 local shell/file path, not end-user UI latency, external LLM latency, database/vector-search performance, or ordinary workflows that do not use this runtime. It is also a single-host, 20-pair result; broader hardware coverage and long-running soak tests would still be needed. I retained the authoritative raw JSON report with SHA-256 `a50cf5d7b4c248aa75286a937bdb1c3e02935e2b88f3c1a340f4c85e3c5c42de`.

## Additional Context

- Rust runtime: formatting and Clippy passed; 4 unit tests passed.

rc core/bwlimit: sub-KiB rate is scaled by 1024 when the reported rate is fed back in

#### What is the problem you are having with rclone?

`BwPair.String()` prints a sub-KiB bandwidth without a unit, and `Set` reads a bare number as KiB, so a bandwidth below 1 KiB is multiplied by 1024 when it goes through a string.

This is the same corruption as 63c4fef27 ("fs: fix corruption of SizeSuffix with `B` suffix in config"), which fixed it for `fs.Option` by suffixing bare numbers with `B`. `BwPair.String()` calls `SizeSuffix.String()` directly, so it never got that treatment.

It shows up on `rc core/bwlimit`, which documents that the returned `rate` uses the same format as the `rate` parameter and as `--bwlimit`:

```
rclone rc core/bwlimit rate=500B
{
    "bytesPerSecond": 500,
    "rate": "500"
}
```

Feeding that `rate` back in gives a limit 1024 times larger:

```
rclone rc core/bwlimit rate=500
{
    "bytesPerSecond": 512000,
    "rate": "500Ki"
}
```

So anything that reads the current limit and writes it back, or restores a saved value, silently raises the limit.

#### What is your rclone version?

master at 4e7a21bea

#### Which OS you are using and how many bits

macOS 15.1, darwin/arm64

#### How to replicate with a test

```go
var tt fs.BwTimetable
tt.Set("500B")          // Tx: 500
printed := tt.String()  // "500"

var got fs.BwTimetable
got.Set(printed)        // Tx: 512000
```

The same holds for `1B`, `1023B`, `1B:2B` and `Mon-10:00,500B`. Values of 1 KiB and above already round trip, because their suffix is not a digit.

I have a fix that moves the `B` suffixing out of `Option.String()` into a `SizeSuffix` method and uses it from `BwPair.String()` too, with a round trip test. Happy to open a PR.

Swarm: container on an overlay network cannot reach an ingress-published port when the service task runs on the same node (29.9.0; worked on 29.7.2)

### Description

After upgrading our Swarm cluster (13 nodes, Ubuntu 24.04.5) from Docker Engine 29.7.2/29.8.0 to 29.9.0, containers attached to an overlay network can no longer establish new TCP connections to a port published through the ingress routing mesh when the service task runs on the same node as the connecting container. The connection attempt times out (ETIMEDOUT).

Connections from containers on any other node to the same published port work fine.
Connections from the host itself (host network namespace) to its own published port work fine. Only containers attached to overlay networks on the same node are affected.
Already-established TCP connections keep working; only new connects fail. This made the problem surface gradually (long-lived DB connections survived, restarted containers could not reconnect).

The problem affects every node in the cluster equally (verified on two different nodes with a minimal reproduction), so it is not corrupted state on a single node. It survives:

systemctl restart docker on the affected node
docker service update --force on the published service and on the client services
a full reboot of the affected node

Last known good version: 29.7.2 (the same workload ran for months with the client containers co-located with the published service). We did not bisect 29.8.x, so the regression is somewhere in 29.8.0–29.9.0.

Possibly related to the fixes that landed in 29.9.0 itself (moby/moby#53723 "published port unreachable from another container ... including Swarm services published through the routing mesh", moby/moby#53663 stale VXLAN FDB entries, moby/moby#53825 DOCKER-INGRESS chain cleanup) — the symptom matches the first one, but on 29.9.0 it is not fixed for the same-node case in our environment.

### Reproduce

Multi-node swarm, default ingress network. NODE_A is any worker, NODE_A_IP its address on the swarm data path. testnet is any attachable overlay network (the same happens with stack-created overlay networks).
`# on a manager
docker network create -d overlay --attachable testnet
docker service create --name lbtest \
  --constraint node.hostname==NODE_A \
  --publish 18080:80 nginx:alpine

# 1) SAME NODE — on NODE_A:
docker run --rm --network testnet alpine \
  sh -c 'wget -qO- --timeout=5 http://NODE_A_IP:18080 >/dev/null \
         && echo SAMEHOST_OK || echo SAMEHOST_FAIL'
# -> SAMEHOST_FAIL   (wget: download timed out)

# 2) OTHER NODE — on NODE_B:
docker run --rm --network testnet alpine \
  sh -c 'wget -qO- --timeout=5 http://NODE_A_IP:18080 >/dev/null \
         && echo REMOTE_OK || echo REMOTE_FAIL'
# -> REMOTE_OK

# 3) HOST ITSELF — on NODE_A (host netns):
timeout 5 bash -c "</dev/tcp/NODE_A_IP/18080" && echo HOST_OK
# -> HOST_OK`

Same result with a MariaDB client container against a published ProxySQL service (ERROR 2002 (HY000): Can't connect to server (110) from the same node, Access denied i.e. successful TCP from any other node).

### Expected behavior

A container attached to an overlay network should be able to reach an ingress-published port regardless of whether the service task runs on the same node or a different one (as it did on 29.7.2).
Observations from the ingress sandbox on an affected node
`# nft DNAT rule for the published port exists and its counter increases
# with every attempt:
nft list table ip nat | grep 3306
  iifname != "docker_gwbridge" tcp dport 3306 counter packets 295311 ... dnat to 172.18.0.2:3306

# (iptables -t nat -L DOCKER-INGRESS prints "Incompatible with this kernel"
#  via the iptables-nft wrapper, but the rules are present in nft.)

# inside the ingress sandbox:
nsenter --net=/var/run/docker/netns/ingress_sbox cat /proc/net/ip_vs
  IP Virtual Server version 1.2.1 (size=4096)
  Prot LocalAddress:Port Scheduler Flags
    -> RemoteAddress:Port Forward Weight ActiveConn InActConn
  FWM  0000015A rr
    -> 0A000013:0000      Masq    1      5          1489

# route to the service's ingress VIP inside the sandbox:
nsenter --net=/var/run/docker/netns/ingress_sbox ip route get 10.0.0.30
  local 10.0.0.30 dev lo src 10.0.0.30

# TCP connect to the VIP inside the sandbox:
nsenter --net=/var/run/docker/netns/ingress_sbox bash -c "</dev/tcp/10.0.0.30/3306"
  Connection reset by peer`

So the DNAT fires, but on the node that hosts the task the IPVS/ingress path does not deliver the connection to the local backend.

bug(scan): single-token content_filter negatives match inside other words ("java" rejects every JavaScript posting)

### What

`buildContentFilter()` in `scan.mjs` matches negative keywords with plain `String.includes()`. Single tokens therefore reject postings that merely *mention* them inside another word:

```js
buildContentFilter({ negative: ['java'] })('We ship TypeScript/JavaScript')
// → false — a Node/TS role discarded because of one substring hit
```

The same collision hits `ios`: a negative `ios` rejects any posting containing the word "curiosity".

Combined with #2695 (discards leave no record), these postings vanish silently.

### Proposed fix

Anchor single tokens at word boundaries (same lookaround discipline `compileLocationKeyword()` already uses, so the two filters can't drift); multi-word phrases like `security clearance` keep exact-substring semantics since those are intended to match anywhere. Genuine standalone mentions still reject: `java` still blocks an actual Java shop, and a real `ios` negative still blocks iOS-only roles.

A tested implementation exists locally (unit tests covering both the anchoring and phrase passthrough); happy to share the diff if a PR isn't wanted from my side.

bug(dashboard): open failures are written to stderr under an active alt-screen, so o/m/d are silent no-ops over SSH

## Summary

`openCmd` reports failures by writing to **stderr while the Bubble Tea alt-screen is active**, so the message is painted over and never reaches the user. The three keys that route through it — `o` (job URL), `m` (manifesto), `d` (open CV PDF) — become silent no-ops on any machine where opening fails, most commonly a dashboard run over SSH.

The correct pattern already exists **25 lines below**, in the same file: `runGeneratePDF` surfaces the identical error as a flash (`"PDF generated but could not open: %v"`). `openCmd` is the one open path that never got it.

## The code

`dashboard/main.go`:

```go
func openCmd(target string) tea.Cmd {
	return func() tea.Msg {
		if err := openWithDefaultApp(target); err != nil {
			fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "WARN: failed to open %q: %v\n", target, err)
		}
		return nil
	}
}
```

The program runs with `tea.NewProgram(m, tea.WithAltScreen())` (main.go:408), so that `Fprintf` is invisible by construction — on every platform, for every failure mode. It is not a headless-specific bug; SSH is just where it is guaranteed to fire.

Meanwhile, in the same file:

```go
if err := openWithDefaultApp(pdfAbs); err != nil {
    return screens.PipelinePDFGeneratedMsg{Err: fmt.Sprintf("PDF generated but could not open: %v", err)}
}
```

…which `Update` turns into a flash at `pipeline.go:477`. So `D` tells you when opening failed; `o`, `m` and `d` do not.

## Reproduction

1. SSH into a machine with no `DISPLAY` (a Pi, a VPS, any headless box) — a TUI is a normal thing to run this way.
2. Run the dashboard, select a row that **has** a URL.
3. Press `o`. Also try `m` and `d`.

Expected: some indication that nothing could be opened.
Actual: nothing at all. No flash, no error, no visible change. Indistinguishable from an unbound key.

## Secondary defect: `xdg-open` exit 0 on failure

For some failure classes `xdg-open` exits **0** while still failing, so `err` is nil and even the (invisible) stderr line never fires. Measured on Debian/xdg-utils:

| target | result | exit |
|---|---|---|
| missing file | correctly reports failure | 2 |
| registered handler that cannot run | prints `Error: no "view" rule for type ... passed its test case` | **0** |

This matters beyond `openCmd`: it means even the correctly-written `runGeneratePDF` path can flash **"PDF regenerated and opened"** when nothing opened. Any fix that only forwards the error will still miss this class.

## Why this isn't already covered

- **#3379** (`'o' doesn't work for entries without reports`) fixed the *empty-`JobURL`* branch and added `m.flash = "No URL found for this application"`. That established flash-on-failure as the intended UX for exactly this key. This issue is the **remaining** branch of the same behaviour: the URL is present, the opener is invoked, it fails, and we are back to a silent no-op.
- **#981 / #980** are about shell-injection hardening of the Windows opener. #981 notes *"Error-propagation for `openNow` was fixed in PR #797"* — correct, but that propagation terminates at `openCmd`'s stderr write, one layer short of the UI.
- **#88** is which command to invoke per-OS, not what to do when it fails.

## Suggested fix

Follow the pattern already in the file rather than inventing one:

1. Have `openCmd` return a message carrying the error (a small `OpenFailedMsg{Target, Err}`, or reuse the existing flash path) instead of writing to stderr.
2. Handle it in `Update` by setting `m.flash`, as `PipelinePDFGeneratedMsg` already does.
3. Because of the exit-0 class above, do not rely solely on the exit code — capture the opener's output, or detect the no-graphical-session case up front (`DISPLAY`/`WAYLAND_DISPLAY` unset on Linux) and report it without shelling out.
4. Optional, but it turns three dead keys into useful ones on remote boxes: include the URL/path in the flash so it can be selected and copied out of the terminal.

Not claiming this one — leaving it for whoever wants it. It should be a well-scoped pickup: the change is confined to `dashboard/main.go` plus one `case` in `pipeline.go`'s `Update`, and the pattern to copy is already in the same file.

## Environment

Raspberry Pi OS (Debian, arm64), Go 1.24.4, xdg-utils; dashboard at v1.31.0, `dashboard/main.go` verified identical on current `main`.

pytest: collecting rag/flow/tests/ together with test/unit_test/rag/ corrupts deepdoc.parser (cascading PlainParser ImportError)

## Summary

Collecting `rag/flow/tests/` and `test/unit_test/rag/` **together in a single pytest invocation** corrupts the cached `deepdoc.parser` package module in `sys.modules`, which then makes **every** `from deepdoc.parser import X` fail with a cascading `ImportError: cannot import name 'PlainParser' from 'deepdoc.parser.pdf_parser' (unknown location)`.

This is **not** a `deepdoc` native-build problem and **not** a bug in any single test file. Each suite collects cleanly on its own.

## Reproduction

Each suite alone is green:

```bash
python -m pytest rag/flow/tests/ --collect-only -q          # 12 tests, OK
python -m pytest test/unit_test/rag/test_naive_merge.py --collect-only -q   # 23 tests, OK
```

Combined collection fails:

```bash
python -m pytest rag/flow/tests/test_token_chunker_tag_overlap.py test/unit_test/rag/test_naive_merge.py --collect-only -q
# ERROR collecting rag/flow/tests/test_token_chunker_tag_overlap.py
# ImportError: cannot import name 'PlainParser' from 'deepdoc.parser.pdf_parser' (unknown location)
```

The failure is **order-independent** (swapping the two args still fails) and **survives `--import-mode=importlib`**.

## Root cause

`PlainParser` is only a symptom. At the moment of failure, `sys.modules` shows:

```
deepdoc.parser.pdf_parser  cached: __file__=None  __path__=None  hasPlainParser=False
deepdoc.parser.__path__=None          # the deepdoc.parser package module itself is broken/partial
deepdoc.__path__=['/home/.../ragflow/deepdoc']   # correct
```

`deepdoc.parser.pdf_parser` has `__file__=None` and its `SourceFileLoader.exec_module` is never invoked, so the real `deepdoc/parser/pdf_parser.py` is never executed — it was cached as a namespace/partial module. Any later `from deepdoc.parser import ...` then fails against this poisoned cache, and the error chain cascades into `docs_generator`, `invoke`, `rag.flow.*`, etc.

The trigger is structural to the test layout:

- `test/unit_test/rag/` and `rag/flow/tests/` are **not packages** (no `__init__.py`). pytest's default `prepend` import mode puts each of these directories on `sys.path[0]`.
- `test/unit_test/rag` is itself named `rag`, and `test/unit_test/` contains a `deepdoc/` directory (`test/unit_test/deepdoc/parser/...`).
- When both suites are imported in one process — the flow suite via `rag.flow.parser.pdf_chunk_metadata → api.db.services → deepdoc.parser`, and the `test/unit_test` suite via `rag.nlp` and its conftest — `deepdoc` / `deepdoc.parser` resolution hits a namespace / partial-module cache collision and `deepdoc.parser` ends up cached as a non-package broken module.

Note: CPython 3.13 executes most of the import machinery in C, bypassing `builtins.__import__`, `module_from_spec`, and `SourceFileLoader.exec_module`, so the precise first corruption event cannot be observed via Python-level import hooks; the `sys.modules` end-state above plus the failure conditions are sufficient to localize the mechanism.

## Independent verification that `deepdoc` is fine

```bash
python -c "import deepdoc.parser.pdf_parser as m; print(m.__file__)"   # OK
python -c "from api.db.services.task_service import TaskService; print('ok')"  # OK
# pure-python: import rag.nlp then import rag.flow.chunker.token_chunker  -> OK
```

## Suggested fixes (out of scope for this issue)

1. **Decouple the import path**: `rag/flow/parser/pdf_chunk_metadata.py` does `from api.db.services.file_service import FileService` at module top level, which pulls in the entire `api.db` stack (and thus `deepdoc.parser`) whenever the chunker package is imported. Moving that heavy import behind a function / lazy import removes the chunker from the `deepdoc` import chain.
2. **Make test directories real packages** (add `__init__.py` to `test/unit_test/rag`, `rag/flow/tests`, etc.) so pytest resolves them unambiguously instead of as `sys.path` roots / namespace portions.
3. **Keep the two suites in separate pytest invocations** in CI as a stopgap (each already collects green alone).

## Workaround for the affected test

`rag/flow/tests/test_token_chunker_tag_overlap.py` collects and passes cleanly **on its own** (and will in CI once `deepdoc` is built). It only breaks when collected in the same process as `test/unit_test/rag/`. No code change is required in that test.

CLAUDE_MEM_CHROMA_ENABLED=false does not stop merged-worktree adoption from spawning chroma-mcp, and worker shutdown then orphans it

**Version:** 13.34.2 (also seen on 13.32.0), macOS (Darwin 25.6, Apple Silicon), bun 1.3.9
**Related:** #3610 (Chroma sidecar contract), #3602 (child process ownership)

### Summary
With `CLAUDE_MEM_CHROMA_ENABLED=false` in `~/.claude-mem/settings.json`, every worker start still spawns chroma-mcp via the merged-worktree adoption pass, which then rewrites the merged-project metadata on all vector documents. Because the flag also leaves `chromaMcpManager` unset, the worker's graceful shutdown never stops that chroma-mcp, so it is left running (~1.2 GB footprint here) and can be killed mid-persist on the next restart.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Set `"CLAUDE_MEM_CHROMA_ENABLED": "false"` and restart the worker.
2. Have at least one worktree that adoption has merged into a parent project.
3. Watch the log and `pgrep -fl chroma-mcp`.

### Observed (13.34.2, worker started 2026-10-06 21:31:48)
- 21:31:48 `Chroma disabled … skipping ChromaMcpManager`, then in the same second `Adopting merged worktrees (background)…`
- 21:32:03 `Connecting to chroma-mcp`, `Removed stale Chroma writer lock (priorPid=8008)`
- 21:53:23 `merged_into_project metadata patched … chromaDocsPatched=88056`, then `Merged worktrees adopted in background … chromaUpdates=12879, chromaFailed=0`
- The same full re-patch happened at the previous start (20:49), even with `adoptedObservations=0`, so every start opens a ~21-minute Chroma write window.
- chroma-mcp then stays resident and idle indefinitely (1241 MB footprint, mostly swapped).

### Cause (from the shipped bundle)
- `scripts/worker-service.cjs`: both adoption paths construct a Chroma client with no flag check, e.g. `new Fi("claude-mem").updateMergedIntoProject(...)`. That client goes through `getInstance()`, which spawns chroma-mcp.
- The flag gates only `ChromaMcpManager` and search.
- The shutdown routine stops chroma only `if (chromaMcpManager)`, which is unset when the flag is off, so the adoption-spawned chroma-mcp is never stopped by the worker.

### Why it matters
- Defeats the documented way to run without Chroma (RAM/swap pressure on small machines).
- An orphaned chroma-mcp killed during that write window is the same mid-persist kill that left us with 1,034 all-zero, id-less HNSW entries and `Error finding id` on every project-filtered query (fixed locally by a full rebuild).
- Re-patching all 88k docs when nothing new was adopted is wasted work on every start.

### Suggested fix
1. Skip the Chroma side of adoption (or defer it to the next Chroma-enabled start) when `CLAUDE_MEM_CHROMA_ENABLED=false`.
2. Make adoption's Chroma re-patch idempotent: only patch when `adoptedObservations > 0` or the merged set changed.
3. Have shutdown stop any chroma-mcp the worker spawned, regardless of how it was spawned (fits #3602).

### Workaround
After `Merged worktrees adopted in background` appears in the log, and once chroma-mcp is idle: `pkill -TERM -f chroma-mcp`.

Current `main` at `fb3d473a73b039251ac8f28297a54d2a89e5d67e` (`2026.7.2` source checkout)

report:
core/state, core/tracing: live tracer state reads are recorded in the block access list, making Amsterdam blocks fail validation

#### System information

Geth version: v1.17.6 (also present on master @ 93d78a01ab)
CL client & version: lighthouse v8.3.0-rc.0
OS & Version: Linux
Network: Sepolia, Amsterdam (activated 2026-10-06 13:53:36 UTC)

#### Summary

We run geth with a live tracer (`--vmtrace`) at Tenderly to index Sepolia and mainnet. At the Sepolia
Amsterdam fork, both of our live-traced nodes stopped importing at block 11856336, the last pre-fork
block, while untraced nodes kept following the chain.

Since Amsterdam, `StateDB` records every account and storage *read* into the block access list
(EIP-7928). The `StateDB` that live tracers receive in `tracing.VMContext` is the same object the EVM
executes on. Any `GetBalance` / `GetNonce` / `GetCode` / `GetState` / `Exist` call a tracer makes from
a hook is therefore recorded in the locally constructed BAL. If the tracer reads an account or slot
that execution itself did not touch, the local BAL hash no longer matches the header, and
`ValidateState` rejects a valid block:

```
access list hash mismatch, local: aa8f…, remote: e604…
```

The node then stalls at the last pre-fork block. Nodes without a tracer are unaffected: they don't
make the extra reads, and they also take the BAL-parallel path. So the failure only appears on nodes
running `--vmtrace`, where it is easy to misread as a consensus bug.

#### Where it happens

- `core/state/statedb.go` `getStateObject` calls `s.stateAccessList.AccountRead(addr)` on every
  lookup once `Prepare` has seen `rules.IsAmsterdam`. `stateObject.GetCommittedState` does the same with
  `StorageRead(addr, key)`.
- `core/state_processor.go` wraps the state in `state.NewHookedState(statedb, hooks)` and builds the
  EVM on it. `EVM.GetVMContext()` then hands that same `evm.StateDB` to `OnTxStart` and
  `OnSystemCallStartV2`. The `tracing.StateDB` interface is read-only, but its reads aren't
  side-effect free.
- `core/blockchain.go` `supportsParallelExecution` disables the BAL-parallel processor whenever a
  tracer is attached, and block import always runs with `EnableTracer: true`. Every live-traced node
  therefore builds its BAL sequentially, with tracer reads included.
- `core/block_validator.go` `ValidateState` compares `res.Bal.ToEncodingObj().Hash()` with
  `header.BlockAccessListHash`.

#### Why this is hard to avoid inside a tracer

Reading state from hooks has been a normal tracer pattern, and the built-in `prestateTracer` and
`erc7562` tracers do it. Under Amsterdam a live tracer may only read an account or slot at a point
where geth has *provably* already read it in the same block. In practice that rule is subtle. We hit
these cases on Sepolia within the first 24h:

1. **System calls.** `OnEnter` for the beacon-root/history/request system calls has
   `from = params.SystemAddress`, but `evm.Call` with `isSystemCall` never reads the caller (it skips
   `CanTransfer`/`Transfer`). Reading the caller's balance adds `SystemAddress` to the BAL.
2. **Frames that fail before touching the callee.** Calls rejected on depth (`> CallCreateDepth`) or on
   `CanTransfer` never read `to`.
3. **Steps reported with an error.** The interpreter's deferred `EmitOpcode` reports a step that
   failed before executing (e.g. OOG on dynamic gas). The operand is visible on the stack, but the
   state read never happened.
4. **Halted top frames.** A type-4 tx whose authorization cannot pay the Amsterdam account-creation
   state gas goes through `applyAuthorizations` → `haltTopFrame`, which emits `OnEnter`/`OnExit(OOG)`
   for a frame that never read the recipient. A tracer reading `tx.To()` in `OnTxStart`, the common
   pattern, adds it to the BAL (Sepolia block 11859740, tx 22, recipient `0x0`).

Each of these is a correct-looking tracer. The block is still rejected, and the node stays stuck even
after the tracer is fixed, until it is restarted (the bad-block mark is in memory).

#### Expected behaviour

Attaching a live tracer has no effect on block validity. Reads a tracer makes through
`tracing.StateDB` are not recorded in the block access list.

#### Actual behaviour

Tracer reads are recorded into the BAL. The block fails `ValidateState` with
`access list hash mismatch`, and the node stops importing.

#### Steps to reproduce

1. On an Amsterdam chain, run geth with a live tracer whose `OnSystemCallStartV2` / `OnEnter` hook
   calls `ctx.StateDB.GetBalance(from)`.
2. Import a block. The beacon-root system call alone is enough: the caller `params.SystemAddress` is
   not in the header's BAL.
3. Import fails with `access list hash mismatch`.

Programmatic reproduction: execute `core.ProcessBeaconBlockRoot` twice on the same state, once with
`vm.Config{}` and once with a tracer whose `OnEnter` reads the caller's balance. Compare
`statedb.Finalise(rules)`/BAL hashes: they differ, and the traced BAL contains `SystemAddress`.

#### Possible paths forward

We'd like a fix in geth rather than every tracer author rediscovering these cases. Options we
considered, roughly from least to most invasive:

**A. Give tracers a non-recording view of the state (preferred).**
`GetVMContext()` returns a thin wrapper instead of `evm.StateDB`. The wrapper serves reads without
calling `stateAccessList.AccountRead` / `StorageRead`, for example through unexported
`getStateObjectNoRecord` / `GetCommittedStateNoRecord` variants, or through a "suspend access recording"
toggle the wrapper sets around each read. This can't be done inside `hookedStateDB` itself, because
the EVM's own reads go through that object too; it needs a separate tracer-facing view.
- Pros: transparent to every existing tracer, no API change, BAL is exactly what execution produced.
- Cons: tracer reads still load objects into `stateObjects` and the reader cache, which is
  state-neutral but not free. The same leak exists for any other read-tracking structure (e.g. witness
  collection, if a tracer is ever combined with `MakeWitness`), so the wrapper should bypass those too.

**B. Restrict tracer reads to what the block already accessed.**
The tracer-facing view answers only for accounts and slots that already appear in the access list,
either the in-flight construction list or, better, the BAL carried in the block body
(`block.AccessList()`). Anything else returns zero, or `(value, false)` via a new
`tracing.StateDB` method.
- Pros: the BAL can never change. Checking against the block's own BAL makes the result independent
  of when in the block the tracer reads.
- Cons: silently returning zero for an unknown account is a semantic trap, so an explicit
  `ok`/error return is better, but that is an interface change. It also doesn't help pre-Amsterdam
  blocks (which aren't affected anyway) or blocks imported without a BAL body.

**C. Skip or relax the BAL hash check when a live tracer is attached.**
For example, an opt-in `--vmtrace.skipbalcheck`, or validating the header BAL with `enc.Validate`
only.
- Pros: trivial and unblocks indexers immediately.
- Cons: a traced node would accept blocks with an invalid BAL, which weakens consensus validation.
  Acceptable at most as an explicit opt-in for nodes that follow a trusted CL and never build blocks.
  We don't think it should be the default.

**D. Suspend BAL recording for the duration of each hook dispatch.**
The `Emit*` helpers, or a `WrapWithJournal`-style wrapper on the live tracer's hooks, set a flag on
the `StateDB` while a hook runs so that nothing it reads is recorded.
- Pros: covers every hook, including reads made through references the tracer kept from an earlier
  `VMContext`.
- Cons: hook dispatch doesn't currently know the `StateDB`, which needs plumbing. It is also easy to
  miss a dispatch site.

**E. Re-validate without the tracer before declaring the block bad.**
On a BAL mismatch with a tracer attached, re-execute the block untraced, or with recording suspended.
If the hash then matches, accept the block and log a loud "tracer-induced BAL divergence" warning.
- Pros: never marks a valid block bad, and makes the cause obvious.
- Cons: doubles the work on the failing path. The tracer already received `OnBlockEnd(err)` for the
  failed attempt and needs a consistent replay.

**F. Document the constraint.**
Whatever the fix, `core/tracing` docs and the live-tracer guide should state that, post-Amsterdam, a
tracer must not read state that execution hasn't touched. The four cases above make useful examples.
On its own this isn't a fix: the cases are too subtle to rely on documentation.

We (Tenderly) are happy to send a PR for **A**, possibly with **B** as an opt-in strict mode, if that
direction sounds right to you. In the meantime we have worked around all four cases in our tracer, but
any other live tracer that reads state is exposed to the same failure on Amsterdam chains.

an issue that data can be lost. (was not there before, can be changes in quic or stream iter).

What the test does is, create a server side unidirectional stream with some bytes and immediately closing the stream.
The client is unable to read the data, because I use:
```
this.readiterator_ = this.stream[Symbol.asyncIterator]()
```
and then later call:
```
 await this.readiterator_.next()
```
when the code needs it.

The problem is, that only at the call to `next()` the async iterator of `QuicStream` is called, that creates the reader on the C++ Stream object.
However, the `#handle` is destroyed once the stream is closed (from the server side) and a later call to `this.readiterator_.next()` can not retrieve that data on client side as the `#handle` is gone, and the data was in its accumulation buffer. 

I can work around this problem, by calling `next()` early and awaiting the promise later. (at least I hope)

But I am wondering, if the lazy allocation of the stream's reader is a good idea. I know from user querys about my webtransport package, that a lot of user use streams to send messages and immediately close them (though I do not like this pattern), but this use pattern may result into the same problem.

### Reproduction steps

I wrote this issue text myself, but my LLM had a diagnosis that I thought sounded reasonable (and I verified the steps it took to test it):
<details>
<summary>LLM diagnosis</summary>

> My diagnosis is that Zed’s workspace-diagnostics timeout is creating a retry loop. Every two minutes, Zed cancels the existing request and starts a new one. Basedpyright treats each new request as a reason to analyze the workspace again, so memory grows with every retry.
>
> I tested this by temporarily preventing repeated requests from starting another analysis. Zed continued to time out and retry—eight times over 17 minutes—but basedpyright settled at about 19 MiB instead of growing toward 3 GiB. This suggests the repeated requests, rather than the project’s size, are causing the growth.
>
> I believe Zed should own the primary fix because it creates and controls the retry loop, and `diagnosticMode: "workspace"` is explicitly supported in Zed’s Python documentation. Basedpyright keeping the request open contributes to the interaction, but that behavior is inherited from Pyright. Zed can prevent the repeated work for both servers by handling a timed-out workspace-diagnostics request without immediately starting the same work again.
>
> For comparison, VS Code’s standard language client leaves the current workspace-diagnostics request open and processes partial results as they arrive. It only starts another request after the current one finishes and does not apply Zed’s 120-second inactivity timeout. This allows basedpyright’s long-running request to remain active without repeatedly restarting workspace analysis. This behavior is visible in [VS Code’s language-client implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-languageserver-node/blob/main/client/src/common/diagnostic.ts#L481-L531).
</details>

Current behaviour: Memory usage grows unboundedly in workspace mode.
Expected behaviour: Memory usage stays roughly flat over time after the initial workspace analysis.
